title: 2 Corinthians 9:6–15
context: Paul grounds Christian giving in God’s generosity. Those who sow bountifully reap bountifully; God loves a cheerful giver and supplies everything needed for good works. The collection meets real needs, produces thanksgiving, and unites the churches, and Paul ends by thanking God for his indescribable gift. Both traditions agree that God’s grace is the source and goal of giving, while describing how grace and the human will relate in different ways.

verses.text: Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever sows sparingly reaps sparingly; whoever sows bountifully reaps bountifully. Arminian readers take the harvest principle as a real link between faithful generosity and God’s rewarding response, without making it a transaction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also affirm the principle and usually stress that the harvest is God’s gracious gift, not a debt owed to the giver. Both traditions reject using this verse to promise guaranteed financial return; the harvest includes spiritual fruit and thanksgiving, as verses 10–12 show.

verses.text: Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verses.arminianNotes: Each should give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under pressure, for God loves a cheerful giver. Arminian readers emphasize the genuine freedom of the giver’s decision; God delights in a willing heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers equally affirm that giving must be willing. They add that a cheerful heart is itself a fruit of grace, as 8:1 and 9:14 suggest. Both agree that coerced giving misses the point.

verses.text: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.
verses.arminianNotes: God is able to make all grace abound so that believers have enough for every good work. Arminian readers see God’s enabling grace equipping believers, who then use what they receive for good works.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers highlight “all grace” and “every good work,” seeing God as the source both of the resources and of the good works themselves. Both agree that God’s sufficiency, not the giver’s wealth, is the foundation of generosity.

verses.text: As it is written, “He has scattered abroad. He has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: Paul quotes Psalm 112:9 about the righteous person who gives freely to the poor and whose righteousness endures. Arminian readers see the generous believer as reflecting the character of the godly person described in the psalm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read “righteousness” here mainly as practical righteousness, a life of justice and mercy, rather than the righteousness credited in justification. Many in both traditions read it this way. The psalm shows that generosity is part of lasting godliness.

verses.text: Now may he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed for sowing, and increase the fruits of your righteousness,
verses.arminianNotes: God, who supplies seed and bread, will multiply their seed and increase the harvest of their righteousness. Arminian readers see God faithfully resourcing those who choose to sow generously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that every part of the cycle, seed, bread, and harvest, comes from God, echoing Isaiah 55:10. The giver is a steward of what God supplies. Both see God as the provider behind every gift.

verses.text: you being enriched in everything for all generosity, which produces thanksgiving to God through us.
verses.arminianNotes: Believers are enriched in every way so they can be generous, and their generosity produces thanksgiving to God. Arminian readers note the purpose of enrichment: not accumulation but generosity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same purpose and stress the final goal, thanksgiving to God. God’s glory is the end of the whole process. This is broad shared ground.

verses.text: For this service of giving that you perform not only makes up for lack among the saints, but abounds also through much giving of thanks to God,
verses.arminianNotes: The collection meets the needs of the saints and also overflows in thanksgiving to God. Arminian readers see giving as ministry with both practical and spiritual effects.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the double outcome too: human need is met and God is glorified. The word for “service” has a sense of public service or worship, which underlines that giving is an act of worship.

verses.text: seeing that through the proof given by this service, they glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Good News of Christ and for the generosity of your contribution to them and to all,
verses.arminianNotes: The Jerusalem believers will glorify God for the Corinthians’ obedience to their confession of the gospel and for their generosity. Arminian readers see giving as evidence that faith is genuine and active.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see generosity as proof of genuine faith, though not its ground. Obedience flows from confession of the gospel. Both traditions agree that the gift also helped unite Jewish and Gentile believers.

verses.text: while they themselves also, with supplication on your behalf, yearn for you by reason of the exceeding grace of God in you.
verses.arminianNotes: The recipients will pray for the Corinthians and long for them because of the surpassing grace of God in them. Arminian readers see God’s grace at work in the Corinthians’ willing response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that Paul credits the Corinthians’ generosity to “the exceeding grace of God in you.” Their giving is God’s work in them. Both agree that the collection deepens love and prayer between churches.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions agree the Corinthians’ generosity is a work of God’s grace. Arminian readers typically understand that grace as enabling a free response that the Corinthians could have resisted; Reformed readers typically understand it as effectively producing the willing response it calls for.

verses.text: Now thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift!
verses.arminianNotes: Paul ends with thanks to God for his indescribable gift. Arminian readers, with most interpreters, take the gift as Christ himself, or God’s saving grace in Christ, the source of all Christian generosity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise usually take the gift as Christ, recalling 8:9, where Christ became poor for our sake. Some read it more broadly as the grace that produces generosity and unity. In either case, God’s giving comes first and grounds every human gift.
